Foam fractionation (FF) is a physiochemical process in which hydrophobic and surface-active molecules are prefer - entially separated from aqueous solution via extraction by rising bubbles that form a foam layer at the aqueous surface. FF has been proven as a potent remediation technology for various types of wastewaters ( Eldib, 1961; Liu, 2013; Huang, 2017; Jia, 2021), and can be operated at all scales. It has the advantages of relatively simple equipment require - ment, low operation cost and energy consumption, and no need of re - agents addition. FF produces a small volume of highly-concentrated PFAS-containing solution that can be disposed or further treated ( Wong, 2001; Backleh-Sohrt, 2005). There have been studies examining the feasibility of FF to remove PFAS from water, often conducted using laboratory-spiked water samples with PFAS concentrations in the range of milligrams per liter (i.e., parts per million, ppm) or micrograms per liter (i.e., parts per billion, ppb) (Lee, 2017). These concentrations levels however do not reflect those often found in environmental samples, usually in the range of nanograms per liter (i.e. parts per trillion; ppt) (Horst, 2020). This treatment method is based on utilizing the property of PFAS molecules having both hydrophilic and hydrophobic components that leads to the concentra- tion of PFAS on the water-air interface. In foam fractionation, PFAS are concentrated in the foam, which forms on the water surface due to provided aeration. The foam is collected by overflow or by suction. The process is most often performed in batch mode ( Lee and Venkatesan, 2024 , Wang et al., 2023 ), although a continuous process is also possible ( Smith et al., 2022 ). The removed collapsed foam (foamate) is further concentrated by subsequent foam fractionation steps ( Burns et al., 2022 ) or treated by electrochemical oxidation ( Smith et al., 2023b ). Along with PFAS removal, other metrics for foam fractionation success include volume reduction factors (VRFs), PFAS enrichment factors (EF), and mass recovery. This phenomenon should be examined in order to determine if harvesting of foam along with the top layer of the water col- umn would provide improved PFAS removal. Although not addressed in the present work, the results point to potential application of FF for PFAS removal for existing treatment trains such as the acti- vated sludge process and reverse osmosis (RO)/ nanofiltration (NF) membrane concentrate treatment. Successful upscaling of continuous FF for municipal leachate and wastewater plants appears promising since existing technology for bubble aeration for waste- activated sludge full-scale processes is very similar, how- ever, efficient methods of foam capture have yet to be developed for large-scale application. Application of the FF process in series should be examined, wherein the foamate volume could be reduced so as to make utili- zation of advanced oxidation or destruction processes economical and avoid PFAS discharge into the environ- ment. Additionally, the total operational cost should be determined in order to make cost comparisons to conven- tional PFAS removal techniques such as GAC and AIX.
